episode.lensDescription: Everything filtered through how it affects actual students.
episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Tuesday, March 17, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, apprenticeships are rapidly expanding beyond traditional construction trades into health care and technology sectors. According to a comprehensive report by Inside Higher Ed, health care apprenticeships have shown 103 percent growth since 2020, reaching 37,346 registered apprentices. This shift challenges long-held assumptions about apprenticeship programs, as only 39 percent of active participants now work in construction while nontraditional sectors accelerate faster.

Women's participation has tripled between 2014 and 2023, reaching 108,140 apprentices, though they represent just 14 percent of total participants. The largest apprentice occupation for women is nurse assistant, while electrician remains the top occupation for men. Completion rates reveal significant equity gaps, with white participants achieving 61 percent completion compared to 46 percent for Black participants and 55 percent for Hispanic participants.

Community colleges are increasingly serving as connective tissue between employers and apprentices, providing instruction while navigating complex credentialing and funding landscapes. Truckee Meadows Community College's Tesla partnership has grown from 85 apprentices in 2023 to over 1,000 completers. Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College's licensed practical nursing program allows students to work full-time while pursuing credentials, addressing workforce shortages in high-demand fields. The expansion reflects broader economic shifts and evolving cultural attitudes about postsecondary training, with federal investment accelerating through $145 million in pay-for-performance incentives targeting sectors like health care, information technology, and artificial intelligence infrastructure.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. today, college sports departments are warning high school recruits to stop using artificial intelligence to create deceptive recruiting videos. According to NJ.com, the use of A.I.-generated content has entered college sports recruiting, prompting athletic departments to address the practice directly. The development represents a new challenge in maintaining integrity within the college recruitment process, as A.I. technology becomes more accessible and sophisticated for creating realistic but fabricated athletic performance footage. Questions remain about how departments will detect such content and what verification processes might emerge.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, Hamdan Bin Mohammed Smart University concluded a strategic visit to Arizona State University aimed at strengthening academic collaboration in artificial intelligence and digital education. According to TechAfrica News, the delegation, led by Chancellor Mansoor Al Awar, met with ASU President Michael Crow and Executive Vice President Chris Howard to explore partnerships supporting the UAE university's School of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation.

The visit included meetings with EdPlus, Knowledge Enterprise, and Enterprise Technology units, providing insights into ASU's experience leveraging digital infrastructure and A.I.-driven systems to scale education. Discussions covered work-integrated learning models, stackable credentials, and flexible professional learning pathways. The delegation toured the Thunderbird School of Global Management and SkySong innovation center to examine university-industry collaboration models. The partnership aims to support the UAE's ambition to position itself as a global hub for digital education and knowledge-driven innovation, though early results suggest implementation challenges remain.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In our Practical Tips category, creating effective A.I.-powered learning personas requires comprehensive character development similar to role-playing games. According to Times Higher Education, educators at Tecnológico de Monterrey developed Anna, a fictional social responsibility consultant who mentors students analyzing companies in crisis. The approach demonstrates how thoughtfully designed A.I. personas can transform simple chat interactions into immersive learning experiences, though questions remain about scalability across different subjects.

The design process begins with creating a complete backstory and world context before developing the A.I. character, ensuring consistent responses aligned with learning objectives. Students first step into junior consultant roles through virtual reality experiences, establishing clear responsibilities before interacting with the A.I. persona. The approach includes risk management through clear boundaries, with guidance for students to provide context, approach advice critically, and protect personal information. Structured debriefs help students examine their reasoning and identify moments when the A.I. challenged their thinking. Early results suggest the strategy transforms A.I. interactions from simple conversations into catalysts for deeper understanding, though educators note that effective learning experiences begin with understanding learners' needs rather than technology alone.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
